memory_update.text: DSGX is the cleanest direct underfollowed public software candidate for the tariff/sanctions/customs/country-of-origin compliance stack because it explicitly sells global trade intelligence, customs/regulatory compliance, denied-party screening, HTS/classification, and export-control tools.

CHRW should be tracked as a logistics-label company with potentially hidden compliance-platform exposure through customs brokerage, tariff advisory content, ACE Import Intelligence, and customs analytics.

EXPD is a reference customs-brokerage and logistics-compliance name; the key later-layer question is whether tariff complexity produces durable customs brokerage profit growth or just offsets freight-cycle pressure.

ULS is a second-order TIC/responsible-sourcing candidate for forced-labor, traceability, supplier audit, and origin-verification compliance; evidence is plausible but requires revenue-line validation.

Many strongest pure-play sanctions screening, forced-labor traceability, and supply-chain illumination vendors appear private or non-US-listed; later passes should check privately held Altana, Assent, QIMA, Kharon, Sayari, Exiger, and others as ecosystem comparables, but they are excluded from this US-listed Layer 1B candidate list.
DSGX should be promoted to the core underfollowed candidate list for tariff/sanctions/customs compliance because the product mapping is direct and public-company exposure is relatively pure.
ULS is a second-order underfollowed candidate for supply-chain compliance and traceability, but requires validation that tariff/origin/forced-labor compliance is material to revenue growth.
EXPD is useful as a customs-brokerage reference name but should not dominate the underfollowed lane because the company is larger and freight-cycle exposure can swamp compliance benefits.
TRI is a direct software/data incumbent through ONESOURCE Global Trade, but the exposure may be diluted at the consolidated company level.

Need a follow-up pass for smaller public vendors in sanctions screening, product traceability, HTS classification, and forced-labor supply-chain mapping; many pure-play leaders appear private or embedded inside larger platforms.

DSGX is the cleanest US-listed underfollowed software/data candidate for the tariff, sanctions, customs, and country-of-origin compliance stack because its products directly cover global trade intelligence, customs/regulatory compliance, tariff/duty data, and denied-party screening.

EXPD and CHRW are second-order logistics-compliance candidates: tariff volatility may not primarily lift freight demand, but can increase customs brokerage, trade consulting, analytics, classification, and restricted-party screening needs.

DNB is a speculative-shadow candidate: sanctions, beneficial-ownership, and supplier-risk data overlap with the compliance stack, but direct customs/tariff exposure must be verified before later-layer survival.

This node appears to split into three investable sub-lanes: direct GTM software/data, logistics customs brokerage/compliance services, and entity/supplier-risk data used for sanctions and restricted-party screening.

E2open/Amber Road would have been a strong US-listed GTM software candidate, but ETWO was acquired by WiseTech Global in August 2025 and is no longer independently US-listed; WiseTech remains a non-US reference anchor rather than a US-listed candidate.

Testing/inspection/certification firms such as SGS, Bureau Veritas, and Intertek have strong traceability and forced-labor compliance relevance but are not clean US-listed small/mid-cap candidates; they may be reference comparables or ADR/OTC watchlist items in a non-US pass.

DSGX is the cleanest US-listed underfollowed candidate for the tariff/sanctions/customs compliance stack because its Global Trade Intelligence products directly map to HS classification, denied-party screening, sanctions content, customs filings, FTZ workflows, and trade-compliance data.

ULS should remain in the adjacent-chokepoint lane: not a tariff software vendor, but a public TIC/supply-chain-assurance company with traceability, responsible-sourcing, social audit, due-diligence, and CTPAT audit services.
EXPD is a reference anchor rather than an alpha-discovery name; customs brokerage is material and filings reference tariff/trade-action complexity, but large-cap freight-cycle factors may dominate.
FWRD is a speculative small-cap shadow candidate with customs-brokerage exposure through logistics operations; needs proof of material compliance revenue before surviving later Serenity layers.

Several highly relevant pure-play compliance/data assets are private or no longer US-listed, including E2open after WiseTech acquisition and Dun & Bradstreet after Clearlake take-private; this makes the public-market map thinner than the private-market evidence map.

For this node, the strongest second-order beneficiary signals should be tracked in product-level KPIs: global trade content updates, restricted-party screening volume, customs-filing workflows, rules-of-origin/FTA tools, traceability audits, CTPAT audits, and trade-compliance consulting demand.
